title: Ten to one, one pH unit
hook: Pour in ten times the acid. Does the pH fall ten times as far?

knows: that a buffer holds a stock of a weak acid and its base (one-dose-of-acid)
that pH is a log scale (ph-log-scale)
doesNotKnow: that a buffer's pH is set by the log of the base-to-acid ratio, not by the amounts

misconception: More buffer, or more of the acid, changes the pH in proportion.
objective: The learner can explain that pH = pKa + log10(base/acid), so an acetate buffer with 10 times as much acid as base has pH about 3.76, one unit below pKa 4.76, and that equal amounts give pH = pKa however much buffer there is.

claims.text: Acetic acid has a pKa of about 4.76 at 25 °C.
claims.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 'Dissociation constants of organic acids in aqueous solution': acetic acid pKa 4.756 at 25 °C.

claims.text: A buffer's pH is pKa + log10(base ÷ acid) (Henderson-Hasselbalch), so 10 times as much acid as base gives about 4.76 − 1 = 3.76.
claims.source: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (Atkins & Jones, Chemical Principles, ch. on buffers; Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. 9). 4.76 + log10(10/100) = 3.76 (node; Demo.tsx pH()).

claims.text: Each tenfold change in the base-to-acid ratio moves the pH by 1; equal amounts give pH = pKa however much buffer there is.
claims.source: From c2: log10(10) = 1; log10(1) = 0 for any equal amounts (10:10 and 100:100 both give 4.76 on the stage).

claims.text: More buffer only makes the pH harder to push (more buffer capacity).
claims.source: Buffer capacity grows with the total buffer concentration (Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. 9, 'buffer capacity'; one-dose-of-acid lesson).

claims.text: The equation holds well for moderate concentrations, about 0.01 to 1 mol/L.
claims.source: Henderson-Hasselbalch neglects water's own ions and activity coefficients; it fails for very dilute buffers or ratios far from 1 (Harris, ch. 9; Po & Senozan, J. Chem. Educ. 78, 1499, 2001). Range quoted as a rule of thumb; the stage's amounts (mmol) are assumed to be in a volume giving such concentrations.

recall.question: A buffer with pKa 7.2 holds 10 times as much base as acid. Its pH is about…
recall.why: pH = pKa + log10(base/acid) = 7.2 + log10(10) = 8.2. A tenfold ratio moves pH by one unit.
